edits.walkthrough_append: Worked check: order six settlements onto the ladder — a 6,000-person notified area (town), a 45,000 municipality (Class III), a 2-lakh city (Class I), and the megacities above ten million at the apex. The ladder matters because functions climb it too: specialist hospitals, universities and corporate headquarters appear only in the upper classes. For the board examination, urban hierarchy questions are answered cold from the thresholds — recall marks — and one step up in reasoning asks which functions a Class III town can and cannot support; answer with the hospital example and the examiner sees the hierarchy, not the memorised table.

Worked check: link each problem to its geography — slums cluster along railway lines, drains and low-lying flood-prone land because that is the land the formal market rejects; congestion concentrates where colonial-era road grids meet modern vehicle numbers; water shortage worsens where the network loses half its supply to leaks. For the board examination, urban-problem answers are graded on the problem-cause-remedy triplet: name slums, congestion, water and sewerage deficits, pollution, and housing shortage; attach one cause each; and close with two remedies at different scales — in-situ slum upgrading and mass transit — rather than a wish-list.

Worked check: differentiate the deficit by region — a Himalayan hamlet's problem is road access across monsoon slips; a Bundelkhand village's is water depth and drought; a Bihar flood-plain settlement's is drainage and embankment Cut-offs. One list of problems, three different first priorities. For the board examination, rural-problem answers earn their marks by organising the deficits into infrastructure, services and livelihoods, illustrating each with a named region, and closing that solutions must be region-differentiated — all-weather roads there, watershed works here — because a uniform programme fixes nothing uniformly.

Worked check: read one smart-city project as a checklist — an integrated command centre reading traffic and utility feeds (smart governance), metered water with leak detection (smart utilities), e-rickshaw charging and feeder buses (smart mobility), and a retrofitted area-upgrade at its core (area-based development). For the board examination, Smart Cities Mission answers give the launch year, the competitive selection of 100 cities, the two strategies — retrofitting or renewal of an area, and pan-city technology — three features with one example each, and the closing critique that smart infrastructure must serve the unstated city, the slum resident, if it is to be called development.

Worked check: reconcile two totals — India's geographical area (about 3.29 million square kilometres) and the smaller reporting area actually recorded in revenue documents, because some forest land and frontier tracts are unreported. Then place the categories: forests, barren and unculturable land, land under non-agricultural uses, pastures, cultivable wasteland, fallow classes, and net sown area. For the board examination, land-use questions ask for the categories from memory and the meaning of reporting area; the sharp answer notes that the missing margin is itself a data problem — plan on the recorded area, but know its boundary.

Worked check: read the shifts as gains and losses in one table — forest cover rising after the 1980 Forest Policy; non-agricultural use (roads, towns, industry) expanding at the expense of the net sown area and pastures; current fallows fluctuating with rainfall; wasteland slowly yielding to reclamation. Each arrow has a policy behind it. For the board examination, land-use-change questions expect the direction of each major shift with one cause each — afforestation programmes, urban sprawl, irrigation expansion — and the closing concern that the sown area is nearly at its ceiling, so future output must come from productivity, not from new land.

Worked check: inventory one village's commons — the grazing pasture, the tank and its catchment, the forest patch for fuel and fodder, the burial ground — and ask who may use what, when, and who polices the rules. Where the community enforces them, the commons last; where they are enclosed or left open-access, degradation follows, and the burden falls on the women and the poor who depend on them most. For the board examination, CPR answers give the definition, three examples, and the two-sided evaluation: equity in access against the tragedy of unmanaged use — with joint forest management as the worked remedy.

Worked check: read the paradox in numbers — a sector employing about 54 per cent of India's workers but contributing only 17-18 per cent of GDP means productivity per agricultural worker is roughly a third of the economy's average; the discrepancy is the agrarian distress in one line. For the board examination, an introduction-to-agriculture answer runs: definition and the types of farming named (subsistence, intensive, plantation), the employment-GDP contrast computed, and the closing implications — disguised unemployment in the fields, the case for non-farm rural jobs, and why output growth must come from yields.

Worked check: match each crop to its map — rice rides the monsoon in the coastal plains and the Brahmaputra valley, climbs the terraces of the hills, and borrows canal water in Punjab's kharif; wheat rules the Ganga-Sutlej plains in winter, needing the cool ripening season and, in the north-west, irrigation's supplement. For the board examination, a rice-versus-wheat answer is a two-column table — season, temperature band, rainfall need, leading states (West Bengal and UP at the top), one each of the cropping patterns — filled line by line; the examiner checks the requirements, so quote them exactly.

Worked check: pair each crop with its dry home — jowar on the Deccan's black soils of Maharashtra, bajra on the sandy Rajasthan plains, ragi on the Karnataka plateau, maize across the kharif belt and as a rabi crop in Bihar, and pulses — gram, tur — as the short-season legumes that fix nitrogen between cereals. For the board examination, coarse-cereal and pulse answers earn marks by the adaptation argument: these are rain-fed crops of marginal lands, drought-hardy and protein-bearing, promoted under the millet missions — one climatic reason per crop is the line that converts a list into an answer.

Worked check: trace each crop to its industry — sugarcane rides the mill's daily crushing radius in UP and Maharashtra; cotton feeds the textile mills of Gujarat and Maharashtra on black-regur soils that hold the monsoon's moisture; jute stays within the Hooghly basin's mill belt because the fibre rets in its water. For the board examination, commercial-crop answers give the crop-condition-industry triangle: each crop's soil and climate in a line, its leading two states, and the processing industry it anchors — that closing industrial link is the mark-earner examiners set the question for.

Worked check: locate by taste of the terroir — groundnut on Gujarat's semi-arid soils, mustard across the rabi plains of Rajasthan and UP, Assam's tea on well-drained slopes under cool, humid shade, coffee under Arabian-sea influence on Karnataka's hills. Two are estate crops (tea, coffee) grown for export; the oilseeds feed the country's edible-oil deficit. For the board examination, commercial-crop answers pair each crop with two states and one condition — soil or climate — and close with the trade angle: tea and coffee earn foreign exchange while oilseeds barely keep imports at bay, which is why the oilseed missions exist.

Worked check: weigh the revolution by its own package — HYV seeds answered only to water and fertiliser, so the gains pooled in irrigated Punjab, Haryana and western UP, in wheat before rice; gains in output and self-sufficiency stand beside falling water tables, soil fatigue, and farm labour left behind where the package could not reach. For the board examination, a Green Revolution answer must carry both columns: achievements (foodgrain growth, buffer stocks, freedom from imports) and critiques (regional inequality, class inequality, ecological cost), because the balanced verdict — success with a footnote of costs — is what the marking scheme rewards.

Worked check: test the system against its three links — the buffer stock: procurement at minimum support price fills it in surplus years; the public distribution system: ration shops move grain to card-holders at issue prices; the safety nets: mid-day meals, ICDS, and the food subsidy that funds the difference. Break one link — procurement fails in a drought year, or grain rots in storage — and security fails downstream. For the board examination, food-security answers define security as availability-plus-access, explain buffer stock and PDS in that order, and close on the NFSA's legal right to food as the reform that made entitlement enforceable.

Worked check: apportion one year's water on paper — of roughly 4,000 cubic kilometres of precipitation, much evaporates, some flows as the rivers' annual run-off, and a fraction recharges the aquifers India pumps hardest; the utilisable slice is far smaller than the total, which is why per capita availability falling towards the stress line matters more than the raw total. For the board examination, water-resources answers carry the sources (precipitation, surface flow, groundwater), the replenishable-versus-non-renewable distinction for deep aquifers, and the closing stress arithmetic: rising population against a fixed utilisable supply is the whole crisis in one ratio.

Worked check: contrast one river from each family — the Brahmaputra, snow-fed and rain-fed, swells catastrophically in flood yet carries navigable and hydro potential; the Narmada, peninsular and monsoon-fed, lives or dies by the season, its west-flowing valley cutting through hard rock in gorges. Himalayan systems feed; peninsular systems depend. For the board examination, drainage answers run the comparison table — source, regime, flood behaviour, utility — line by line with named rivers, and the examiner's closing point is yours to make: the two families demand two water strategies, storage in the south, moderation and management in the north.

Worked check: read one season on the gauge — the monsoon delivers most of the year's rain in under four months, and a shift of two weeks or a break of seven days within it turns a normal year into a drought warning; Cherrapunji's total and Rajasthan's near-zero fall on the same seasonal system. For the board examination, variability answers state the concentration in time and space, give the extremes as evidence, and close with the management consequence — storage, canals and groundwater are the bridges across the monsoon's gaps, which is why irrigation is the largest use of water in the country.

Worked check: stack the objectives on one dam — the reservoir stores monsoon water for canal irrigation; the fall through the turbines generates peak-hour power; the spillway tames the flood that once swept the plain; the pool above feeds fish, the season's boats carry tourists, and the regulated flow supplies drinking water downstream. Each benefit has its ledger entry: submergence, displacement, and the silt that slowly eats the storage. For the board examination, multipurpose-project answers define the integration, list four objectives with one sentence each, and balance them with the costs — that balance is the answer's spine.

Worked check: profile one project fully — the Bhakra Nangal: dam on the Sutlej, reservoir behind it, canals greening Punjab and Haryana, turbines lighting five states, floods blunted between — then one sentence each on the Damodar Valley Corporation as the flood-control model and Hirakud on the Mahanadi as the longest main dam of its era. For the board examination, a major-projects answer is graded on specifics: name, river, states served, two purposes in operation, one displacement-or-siltation cost acknowledged; examiners read the numbers, and a profile with real names outranks any number of generic paragraphs.

Worked check: follow the water's journey — headworks at Harike on the Sutlej-Beas confluence, the main canal running south through Punjab into Rajasthan for hundreds of kilometres, feeding branch canals that carry drinking water and irrigation into the Ganganagar and Bikaner tracts where rain barely crosses 20 centimetres. The canal made settlement possible where sand was sovereign — and brought waterlogging and salinity where application outran drainage. For the board examination, canal answers state the source, the states served, the transformation achieved, and the caution of over-irrigation in one closing line — the full cycle in four sentences.

Worked check: size one rooftop — a 100-square-metre roof under 600 millimetres of harvestable rain collects about 60,000 litres a year; two storage tanks and a recharge pit turn that into a household's drinking buffer and a neighbourhood's dried borewell revived. For the board examination, rainwater-harvesting answers name the techniques — rooftop collection into tanks, recharge pits and trenches, percolation tanks on farmland, and the revival of traditional structures such as tankas and johads — and close with the two-fold purpose: storage for use and recharge for tomorrow, since harvesting is as much about the aquifer as the bucket.

Worked check: audit one use at a time — irrigation takes the lion's share, and drip and sprinkler systems cut its appetite by half against flood fields; cities lose a fifth of supply to leaking mains before a drop is drunk; industry recycles what regulators insist upon; and households answer with rainwater structures and grey-water reuse. For the board examination, conservation answers are graded on measures-per-sector with one saving each — efficient irrigation, leak repair, recycling, harvesting — plus the institutional layer of watershed programmes and pricing, closing that conservation is many small saved litres, not one large dam.

Worked check: read one dispute on its facts — the Cauvery: upstream Karnataka and downstream Tamil Nadu divide a river whose flows fall short in deficit years; tribunals awarded shares, tempos flared when the monsoon failed, and implementation of the final award remains the friction. Compare the Krishna tribunal's basin-wide allocation and the Himalayan treaties negotiated between states. For the board examination, water-dispute answers carry the river, the parties, the tribunal and the crux — upstream storage versus downstream rights — plus the constitutional route under the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, and the closing line that scarcity turns legal shares into annual politics.

Worked check: balance one dam's ledger — against irrigation, power, flood moderation and water supply, set the submerged forest and farmland, the displaced households awaiting rehabilitation, the sediment steadily trading storage for silt, and the seismic and ecological questions raised in movements such as the Narmada Bachao Andolan. For the board examination, dams answers must run both columns to full marks: the multipurpose benefits in four lines, the costs in three, and a closing judgement that dams are instruments whose value depends on siting, rehabilitation and catchment care — not a verdict for or against the idea itself.
